# The Lantern at Wuyang Bridge

In the waning years of the Tang Dynasty, when the imperial roads were thick with bandits and the rice fields lay fallow, there lived a scholar named Li Wenshu who failed his civil examinations three times. Disgraced, he traveled south to teach village children, hoping the mountain air might clear his troubled mind.

His path led him through Wuyang, a hamlet pressed against a slow green river. The villagers warned him not to cross the old stone bridge after dark.

"A woman waits there," said the innkeeper, refusing to meet his eyes. "She carries a red lantern. Do not look at her face."

Li Wenshu, who prided himself on Confucian rationality, laughed politely and paid for his wine.

It was the seventh month—the Ghost Month—when he found himself returning late from a neighboring village, having lost track of time over a game of weiqi. The moon was a thin sickle. Mist rose from the rice paddies like the breath of sleeping things.

At the bridge, he saw her.

She stood at the center of the span, a young woman in mourning white, holding a paper lantern that glowed deep crimson. The light fell only on her hands—small, pale, perfect hands—while her face remained veiled in shadow beneath an elaborate coiffure.

"Honored sir," she said, and her voice was like silk drawn through cold water. "Would you walk an unfortunate woman home? The road is dark."

Li Wenshu remembered the innkeeper's warning. But he also remembered his three failures, his empty purse, his loneliness. And her hands were so very lovely.

"I would be honored," he said, keeping his eyes lowered.

They walked. She spoke of poetry—Li Bai, Du Fu, verses he himself loved. She knew the classics better than any woman he had met. When she laughed, it sounded like distant temple bells.

"My house is just ahead," she said at last.

He looked up despite himself.

The house was a ruin. Black timbers clawed at the sky. Weeds grew through the threshold. And in the doorway, the lantern light at last touched her face—

It was beautiful. Heartbreakingly so. But her eyes held no whites, only deep wells of darkness, and when she smiled, he saw that her teeth were the small, sharp teeth of a child who had died long ago.

"My husband killed me here," she whispered, "sixty autumns past. He poured the wine, and I drank, and the world turned cold. Every night I wait at the bridge for him to walk me home. Every night I forget that he is dust."

Li Wenshu could not move. The lantern's red light pulsed like a slow heart.

"You are not him," she said softly. "But you have his sorrowful eyes. Stay with me, scholar. Only until morning. I am so very tired of walking alone."

What Li Wenshu did next, the villagers would debate for generations.

Some say he fled, and was found at dawn with white hair and a mind emptied of all learning, muttering only of red lanterns until his death.

Others say he stayed. That he sat with her through the night and listened to her tell the whole story of her life—the silk merchant father, the cruel husband, the cup of poisoned plum wine. That at sunrise, she bowed to him with tears like pearls, and dissolved into the morning mist, finally released.

The innkeeper, who outlived them all, claimed only this: that for many years afterward, travelers crossing Wuyang Bridge at night would sometimes see two lanterns moving together along the far bank—one red, one white—and hear the soft sound of two voices reciting poetry to the indifferent stars.

And if you listened closely, the innkeeper said, you could tell that one of the voices was smiling.
